content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a new dataset for video montage generation with 4,356 text-video pairs. The text-video pairs in the dataset are excerpts from some documentaries, where the text is (perhaps) the corresponding subtitles. Some inappropriate pairs are manually removed from the dataset. The paper also presents a method for video montage generation with two training objectives. The first objective penalizes insertion of off-topic shots, while allowing removal of some shots. The second objective is to arrange shots in the order of ground-truth. The paper claims that all these components are the contribution.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths:

I believe a new publicly available dataset can be a nice contribution. Also, the method proposed in the paper makes sense, and the experimental results and the ablation study support the paper’s claims. 

### Weaknesses:

However, although I think the dataset can be a contribution, what the dataset (and the task) offers to the community is not clear enough. I can easily imagine that video montage generation is a highly subjective task, in which there can be multiple ground-truth sequences that are almost equally good, and aesthetics also matter a lot. In this sense, this dataset involves not only a deep understanding of videos and text for their alignment but also some other factors, which may just complicate the task or can be a shortcut to facilitate the prediction. The paper could be better if it included some discussions on this point. 

Related to this, to show the impact of subjectivity, the paper may benefit from some additional user studies. For example, in order to see the subjectivity in shot selection, how well people can find the ground-truth shots from (a subset of) the candidates can be interesting. Evaluating the human’s ability to arrange the ground-truth shots into the correct order can also be useful to show the subjectivity of the task. If people do well in such evaluations, we can see that the dataset is beneficial to evaluate a model’s ability to align shots and text. Otherwise, it’s hard to see what is actually evaluated. 

Also, I think the value added to this dataset compared to the original videos looks limited. Firstly, the number of video-text pairs is relatively small. Secondly, the dataset construction only requires the curation of videos and the removal of some inappropriate pairs. Evaluation of the dataset mentioned above or filtering them to reduce subjectivity may offer additional values, but in the current form, I have to say that the contribution of the dataset is weak.

The design of the CSR task is not obvious. If I understand correctly, the length $n$ of a sequence (the number of shots in the sequence) can vary in this task. If this is the case, I don’t see how the FC in Eq. (10) is handled. Moreover, it’s hard to see what this task offers as supervision. I guess the model uses position embedding, so the order matters in the training, but the sequence is shuffled in the training process, so the position embedding seems meaningless. I would like to have a deeper interpretation of this CSR task. 

As a minor point about CMSM, since positive samples always have more shots while negative samples have fewer, I would like to see the distributions of the lengths of sequences of positive and negative samples and a discussion about how the difference in the length distributions affects the training.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The presentation of the paper is clear enough to understand what is done, and the results can be easily reproduced once the dataset is available. However, due to some missing evaluations about the dataset itself mentioned in the weakness section, the novelty of the task is hard to evaluate. The model is not novel, while the CMSM and CSR tasks seem new in the paper. But the CSR task is not sufficiently justified nor explained, so its importance is not evident.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is trying to address a challenging problem of video montage generation; however, what the dataset (task) actually offers is not clear enough. Also, CSR is underexplained, and hard to evaluate its importance. Although I believe dataset construction can be a contribution, this time, the value added to the dataset is limited.

content.title: Response to Reviewer kWC4 - Part 3/3
content.comment:
**Q5. [As a minor point about CMSM, since positive samples always have more shots while negative samples have fewer, I would like to see the distributions of the lengths of sequences of positive and negative samples and a discussion about how the difference in the length distributions affects the training.]** \
**A5:** Good question. I have to point out that the positive samples always have less shots than negative samples, because we create a positive sample by masking the tail shots of the original video while inserting shots from another video to the original video to create a negative sample. To investigate how the difference in the length distributions affects the training, we conduct two experiments below: 
1. Firstly, we modify the constraint of the random number $L_0$ to $0 \leq L_0 < n/2$, so that the positive samples contain more shots (denoted as 'Pos More').
2. Secondly, we modify the constraint to the length of negative samples (denoted as 'Neg More'). If the length of the selected unpaired shot sequence is less than (or equal to) 5, we directly insert the whole sequence into the paired shot sequence in a random position. If the length of the unpaired sequence is greater than 5, we follow the statement in Section 4.2 in the main paper to obtain a sub-sequence of it but guarantee the sum of $k+L_1$ is greater than 5.

Furthermore, we provide the mean and standard deviation of each length distribution as follows:

| Method   |    Positive     |     Negative    |
| -------- | --------------- | --------------- |
| Pos More | 3.06 $\pm$ 2.24 | 5.43 $\pm$ 2.70 |
| Neg More | 2.57 $\pm$ 1.97 | 6.84 $\pm$ 2.28 |
| RATV     | 2.57 $\pm$ 1.97 | 5.43 $\pm$ 2.70 |

The obtained results for different length distributions are provided below:

| Method | IoU   | UMS   | SMS   |   CS  |
|   ---  | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
|Pos More| 0.119 | 4.240 | 0.076 | 0.453 |
|Neg More| 0.109 | 4.527 | 0.073 | 0.426 |
|  RATV  | **0.144** | **3.393** | **0.090** | **0.685** |

We can observe that both reducing and expanding the difference between the distributions of the lengths of sequences of positive and negative samples make the results worse, which indicates that the difference in the length distributions indeed affects the training and the intuitive setting of our RATV can achieve the best results. In addition, these results also demonstrate that our RATV can indeed learn the knowledge to generate video montage well from give texts, but not shortcut about the difference in the length distributions. We have added these discussion in Appendix H.

content.title: Additional Response to Reviewer kWC4
content.comment:
Thanks for your detailed feedback. We are glad to see that our response addresses most of your concerns. For your most concerned problem with A1, our detailed answers are as follows:

The machine learning models need to learn to create well-edited video montages for this generation task, which should consider not only the understanding of video-text alignment, but also other factors (e.g., temporal coherence and aesthetics). The reasons why we evaluate the models with predefined ground truth per input are:

1. Note that other multi-modal generation tasks (e.g., image caption, video caption, and text-to-image generation) also face the same challenge that there exist multiple ground truths that are almost equally good (but can be totally different) for a single input. Nevertheless, in these tasks, the generation ability is still evaluated with pre-defined ground truth per input. In this work, we thus follow this common practice to exploit pre-defined ground truth (per input) for performance evaluation in the video montage generation task.
2. Although only one pre-defined ground truth is provided for each text script during dataset construction (like text-to-image generation), the models for video montage generation trained on our whole dataset can still acquire the general professional video editing skill, which is essentially inherited from a number of different experts included in dataset construction. This means that the generation diversity can still be ensured for the models trained on our dataset. Additionally, this diversity has been observed in the demo videos generated by our proposed method.
3. It is a good advice to construct a dataset for video montage generation to include multiple ground truths for each text script. However, such dataset construction is very challenging and time-consuming. We thus leave it to our ongoing work.

The above discussion will be updated in our final version.

content.title: Response to Reviewer kWC4 - Part 2/3
content.comment:
**Q3. [I think the value added to this dataset compared to the original videos looks limited. Firstly, the number of video-text pairs is relatively small. Secondly, the dataset construction only requires the curation of videos and the removal of some inappropriate pairs. Evaluation of the dataset mentioned above or filtering them to reduce subjectivity may offer additional values, but in the current form, I have to say that the contribution of the dataset is weak.]** \
**A3:** Please note that there are no available datasets devoted to video montage generation, and existing public video datasets for other tasks are not suitable for this task. To facilitate the research on video montage generation, we construct a new dataset which consists of 4,365 video-script pairs (including 35,045 shots in total). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first public dataset devoted to video montage generation, which has been released at https://github.com/RATVDemo/RATV.

Although we desigh rules to automatically create video-script pairs from documentaries (details are given in Appendix C), we still need to manually process all video-script pairs again to further guarantee the selected video-script pairs are semantically consistent. Our contributions on dataset constrcution are summarized as follows:
* We have reduced the subjectivity when constructing the dataset by carefully selecting videos from documentaries. The suggested user study also shows that our VSPD dataset is beneficial to evaluating a model's ability of video montage generation (see **our response to Q2**). 
* We have filtered the inappropriate pairs, added missing shots to the shot sequences, and removed unmatched shots from shot sequences, which is rather time-consuming and requires much hard work. 
* We have established a benchmark  for video montage generation by re-implementing existing methods on our VSPD dataset as baseline methods. This benchmark will facilitate the research on video montage generation.
 
Overall, our dataset construction requires much hard work, and our contributions on dataset constrcution are sufficient for the community.

**Q4. [The design of the CSR task is not obvious.]** \
**A4:** Thanks for poninting this out. As the reviewer stated, the length of a sequence can vary in this task and the output dimension of FC thus can not be defined. To address this issue, we follow previous transformer-based methods to set a max-length hyper-parameter $L_{max}$. If the length of input shot sequence is less than $L_{max}$, we pad the sequence so that its length is equal to $L_{max}$, and mask the padding tokens when the sequence is fed into the Sequence Consistency Transformer. If the length of input shot sequence is greater than $L_{max}$, we truncate the sequence so that its length is equal to $L_{max}$. With this setting, the FC layer is defined for the $L_{max}$-class classification task, which takes the position of each input token in the original sequence (before shuffling) as the supervision. 

Note that we adopt the position label as the supervision (instead of the position embedding), which can be derived before shuffling the sequence and is not changed during shuffling. For example, we define the original input shot sequence as [0,1,2,-1,-1], where -1 denotes the masked token. We then shuffle the sequence into [2,0,1,-1,-1]. The supervision of the first token in the shuffled sequence is the position label 2. We have added more clear interpretation of the CSR task in Section 4.3 in the main paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer kWC4 - Part 1/3
content.comment:
Thank you for the constructive comments and suggestions.

**Q1. [However, although I think the dataset can be a contribution, what the dataset (and the task) offers to the community is not clear enough. I can easily imagine that video montage generation is a highly subjective task, in which there can be multiple ground-truth sequences that are almost equally good, and aesthetics also matter a lot. In this sense, this dataset involves not only a deep understanding of videos and text for their alignment but also some other factors, which may just complicate the task or can be a shortcut to facilitate the prediction. The paper could be better if it included some discussions on this point.]** \
**A1:** Thanks for this insightful suggestion. As the reviewer stated, video montage generation is a highly subjective task, in which there may exist multiple generated samples that are almost equally good. Therefore, establishing a dataset to well evaluate this task is extreme challenging. 

To alleviate this issue, we choose to collect video-script pairs from well-edited videos (by the experts) including movie, cartoon and MV. However, these three types of videos are not good choice, and the reasons are given below:
* The captions of movie and cartoon are commonly not consistent with the shots because most captions of them are dialogues. 
* The shots in MV are often not temporally coherent. 

In this paper, we thus propose to collect the video-script pairs from documentaries, whose captions are descriptive and consistent with the temporally consecutive shots (as stated in Section 3 in the main paper). More importantly, the documentaries are commonly shot and edited by the experts that have professional expertise. Therefore, the collected videos (i,e., the continuous clips of documentaries) in our VSPD dataset can indeed be considered as the perfect videos w.r.t. semantic consistency, temporal coherence and aesthetics. That is, they can be used as the ground-truth for training and evaluation on the video montage generation task. 

In conclusion, our VSPD dataset is benificial to performance evaluation for video montage generation, which is indeed a contribution to the community. We have added more discussions on this point in Appendix C.

**Q2. [To show the impact of subjectivity, the paper may benefit from some additional user studies.]** \
**A2:** Good suggestion! We conduct the suggested user study to investigate whether people can achieve the goal of video montage generation well on our VSPD dataset. The details of such user study are given below:
1. Note that it is very time-consuming for volunteers to select desired shots according to the give texts from all candidates in the test set of VSPD, which consists of about 800 shots. Therefore, to make the user study more feasible, we randomly select 50 video-script pairs from the test set to construct a subset for user study, which consists of 179 shots. 
2. We then invite 5 volunteers to manually select shots from candidates according to given texts, and arrange selected shots. Specifically, we shuffle the 50 texts and then averagely divide these texts into 5 parts. Each volunteer is given 10 texts in one part, and is asked to select shots from candidates according to each text and arrange the retrieved shots to form a consecutive video. 
3. The resultant IoU and SMS are **0.728** and **0.558**, respectively. Note that the volunteers are not the experts in video editing. Therefore, these two results indicate even inexperienced people that lack professional expertise can still find the ground-truth shots from the candidates and arrange the retrieved shots in the correct order well. 

The user study thus demonstrates that our VSPD dataset is indeed beneficial to evaluating a model's ability of text-shots alignment and shot sequence arrangement. Furthermore, as emphasized in our response to Q1, the videos in VSPD are continuous clips of documentaries, which are well edited by the experts that have professional expertise. Therefore, the impact of subjectivity is relatively minor in VSPD. The results of the user study and the detailed discussion have been added in Appendix G.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes 1) A method that aligns text script and movie shots in a temporally coherent way, and 2) A dataset and benchmark that enables the study of temporally coherent video shot retrieval methods from multiple captions. The proposed method combines text and video encodings into a single sequence that is input into a sequence consistent transformer. This sequence consistent transformer is trained with a combination of text-video alignment and video shot sorting objectives denoted as CMSM and CSR. The authors show that the proposed method outperforms previous approaches that are not specifically trained for aligning scripts and video shots. They show a study where only a single text input is provided to retrieve a video shot all the way to multiple text inputs to highlight the advantage the proposed model has as the text inputs become longer.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Weaknesses / Comments:

- Difference between using CMSM and CMSM + CSR is marginal:
From looking at the ablations, the CSR object provides a very marginal improvement over the CMSM objective, and I wonder whether this is significant enough to add the additional complexity to the overall model. Can the authors comment on this? or provide additional evaluations or analysis that shows that CSR is worth the additional difficulty added during training?

- How are the baselines trained?
I am not sure if I missed this or not, but did the authors train the proposed method and the baselines with the same datasets? It would not be fair if the baselines are evaluated on a different data distribution that they were trained on while the proposed method is. I would like the authors to clarify this.

- Reproducibility:
It seems that the details of the Sequence Consistency Transformer network are missing from the manuscript. Can the authors provide these for replication purposes? Or make it more clear if it is in the text and I just didn't find it?


Questions:
* In Section 4.1, it is mentioned that the model supports zero, one or multiple shots as input. My question is, why would you want to allow zero shots? Isn't it ok if we assume at least one shot?

content.title: Response to Reviewer 7B6W
content.comment:
Thank you for the constructive comments and suggestions.

**Q1. [Difference between using CMSM and CMSM + CSR is marginal.]** \
**A1:** Thanks. We devise the CSR task to encourage the model to learn the reasonable order of shots in a well edited video, so that the model can consider the temporal coherence in addition to semantic consistency. As a result, adding CSR to CMSM only leads to marginal gains in terms of semantic consistency (1.4% relative improvement on IoU and 4.0% relative improvement on UMS in Table 3). However, in terms of temporal coherence, the CSR task helps our RATV achieves significant gains, i.e., it yields 8.4% and 6.2% relative improvements on SMS and CS, respectively.

**Q2. [How are the baselines trained? ]** \
**A2:** Good question. We have provided the implementation details of baselines in Appendix B. All methods (including baselines and our RATV) are retrained or finetuned on the proposed VSPD dataset for fair evaluation. In addition, the implemention details of Write-A-Video and Transcript-to-Video are also given in our resonpse to Q1 of Reviewer s74o.

**Q3. [The details of the Sequence Consistency Transformer network.]** \
**A3:** Sorry for this confusion. In this work, we adopt 2-layer (with 512 hidden units and 8 heads) transformer as our Sequence Consistency Transformer. These details have been updated in Appendix B. Additionally, we have provided the code in the supplementary material, and the details can be found in the file models/cotransformer.py (see lines 17-65).

**Q4. [Why would you want to allow zero shots?]** \
**A4:** Thanks. We have removed this term in the main paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer GsLm
content.comment:
Thank you for the comments and suggestions.

**Q1. [The CMSM and CSR tasks are not well defined and explained]** \
**A1:** Sorry for the confusion. Nevertheless, we have tried our best to make them as clear as we can. As all other reviewers think this paper (including the method part) is easy to understand, could you please point out what is unclear? Thanks.

**Q2: [The motivation for the proposed method is not clear. The proposed method is not well described and is not reproducible.]** \
**A2:** Thanks for pointing this out. With the rapid development of video sharing websits, numerous video content creators desire to create attractive video montage. However, creating a well edited video montage is challenging for most of users due to the lack of professional expertise and aesthetic knowledge for video editing. Therefore, the automatic video montage generation is becoming a popular but challenging task. Given that this is a relatively new task, there is neither available public datasets devoted to it, nor effective methods to well meet its requirements. Motivated by this, we construct **the first public dataset for video montage generation**, and also propose a novel model to overcome the drawbacks of previous methods, which outperforms the state-of-the-art methods with large margins. In addition, we have provided the code in the supplementary material, and we believe that our proposed method is easy to reproduce.

**Q3: [The value added to this dataset compared to the original videos looks limited. but can be a contribution.]** \
**A3:** Please note that the dataset construction for video montage generation requires much hard work, other than only limited value being added to the original videos as stated by the reviewer. Our contributions on dataset construction are three-fold:
1. We have carefully investigated which type of videos is suitable for video montage generation, and proposed to collect video-script pairs from documentaries to reduce the subjectivity. The results of the user study suggested by Reviewer kWC4 demonstrate the soundness of our dataset construction (see our response to Q2 of Reviewer kWC4).
2. After automatically creating video-script pairs from documentaries with rules (stated in Appendix C), we have filtered the inappropriate pairs, added missing shots to the shot sequences, and removed unmatched shots from shot sequences. This is rather time-consuming and requires much hard work. 
3. We have established a benchmark for video montage generation by re-implementing existing methods on our constructed dataset. This benchmark will facilitate the research on video montage generation. 

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first public dataset devoted to video montage generation, which has been released at https://github.com/RATVDemo/RATV.

**Q4: [There is no detailed analysis of the proposed transformer model, and detailed hyper-parameter setting to reproduce]** \
**A4:** Thanks. We propose the Sequence Consistency Transformer to model the consistency of the multi-modal sueqnces containing sentences and shots, and devise two novel tasks for training it so that it can better learn sentence-shot alignment in sequence-level. To investigate the effectiveness of the two novel tasks, we have conducted extensive ablation studies (see the results in Table 3 in the main paper). Furthermore, we have also analysised the influence of the length of input texts in Figure 4. Additionally, the detailed hyper-parameters are given in Appendix B, and **the code is now available in the supplementary material**. 

**Q5: [The experimental results are not very convincing]** \
**A5:** In this paper, we employ exisiting cross-modal retrieval methods and the state-of-the-art mothods for video montage generation as baseline methods. All cross-modal retrieval methods are pre-trained or fintuned on VSPD for fair comparison. We replace the retrieval model of video generation methods with CLIP and fintune their arrangement models on VSPD with frozen CLIP (the same as our RATV). The implementation of the baseline methods have been provided in Appendix B. In addition, the code is now available in the supplementary material. We believe it is easy to reproduce the proposed method with the given code and dataset.

content.title: Further Response to Reviewer GsLm
content.comment:
Thanks for your feedback. For your concerned problems, our detailed answers are as follows:
1. Note that most of existing video datasets are relatively small. For example, the wide-used text-to-video retrieval dataset MSRVTT [1] only consists of 10K shots and Didemo [2] consists of 27K shots. However, our newly constructed dataset consists of 35,045 shots in total. Therefore, it is unreasonable to say that our dataset is too small to validate the effectiveness of our model.
2. Please also note that proposed VSPD is the first dataset devoted to video montage generation. There is **no** existing public datasets that can be used to well evaluate this task, including the datasets suggested by the reviewer (**see A1 in our second-round response**). For the VIST dataset newly mentioned by the reviewer, each sample of VIST consists of only consecutive **text-image pairs**, instead of text-video pairs. Therefore, it is also not suitable for evaluation in **video** montage generation.
3. We have to clarify that our proposed RATV learns not only the documentary's temporal coherency, but also visual-text alignment, aesthetics and other factors simultaneously (instead of only temporal coherency stated by the reviewer). To the best of our knowledge, there is no suitable benchmark to evaluate such task, and we thus propose the VSPD dataset. Reviewer kWC4 also agree the further user study suggested by him has demonstrated our VSPD is valuable and reliable (**see A2 in our first-round response to reviewer kWC4**). And we have made our code and dataset public.

We wish that our response has addressed your concerns to turn your assessment to the positive side. If you have any questions, please feel free to let us know during the rebuttal window. We appreciate your suggestions and comments! Thank you!

[1] MSR-VTT: A large video description dataset for bridging video and language. In CVPR, pages 5288–5296, 2016\
[2] Localizing moments in video with natural language. In ICCV, pages 5804–5813, 2017

content.title: Additional Response to Reviewer GsLm - Part 1/2
content.comment:
Thanks for your feedback. We are glad to see that our response addresses all your concerns. For your newly-raised problems, our detailed answers are as follows: 

**Q1:** I was only able to confirm that temporal coherency was addressed well in this documentary video, but there are other previous works on video retrieval with coherency, which are not compared in other dataset such as ActivityNet, dense video captioning. In this sense, the model should be evaluated on raw footage data or youtube video in the wild to construct a montage in need, but the model retrieves coherent subshot in a small set of the shot candidates in 200 GT well-made subshot in the test set, which is not given always for real applications.\
**A1:** 
1. Note that the video montage generation task requires to retrieve multiple shots and arrange them in a reasonable order with coherent scripts, which includes both retrieval and arrangement tasks. Different from our task, the previous works on video retrieval with coherency mentioned by this reviewer focus on retrieving only one (ground-truth) shot with multiple sentences. 
2. Due to the difference between these two tasks, the datasets devoted to video retrieval are not suitable for video montage generation. For example, each video in ActivityNet contains only one shot that describes continuous actions, and the captions of each video are not temporally coherent, which do not meet the requirements of video montage generation. ActivityNet is thus not suitable for video montage generation.
3. Video montage generation requires to retrieve shots from a shot gallery to assemble them into a complete video. Note that constructing such a shot gallery (that consists of only videos) is not challenging in practice. However, collecting temporally coherent and semantically aligned video-script pairs for evaluation is challenging, especially from Youtube in the wild. As a result, we construct the VSPD dataset from documentaries for evaluation in this paper, and leave the wild dataset construction to future work.

**Q2:** I was able to identify some weird coherency between automatically devided subshot in the shared documentary dataset. (shots 241 - 248)\
**A2:** Thanks for pointing this out. We check the mentioned samples. However, we regret to say that we did not find any weird coherency problem. Could you please tell us where is weird so that we could further improve our work. Thanks! 

**Q3:** Some single-shot samples can hardly be viewed as montage qualitatively. (shot 18820)\
**A3:** Video montage generation aims to generate a temporally and semantically coherent video given an input script, no matter how many shots are included. This means that the model may generate a video that contains only one shot, if the input script is very simple. As a result, single-shot samples are meaningful for video montage generation.

**Q4:** Some data are just natural sorting of automatically divided subshots which is not reliable. and I doubt human screening on this evaluation set.\
**A4:** As mentioned by the reviewer, the automatic processing makes the coherency of video clips worse sometimes. Therefore, we manually process the video-script pairs after automatic processing to further guarantee the coherency of video clips and video-script alignment (**see our first-round response to Q3**).

**Q5:** In addition to this, there is an unnaturalness caused by the division into sentences. It was hard to find some rule. Rather, it was close to the natural alignment of the script and documentary video shot. \
**A5:** The video clips of documentaries are well aligned with the scripts as they are well edited by experts. As a result, we follow the nature alignment in original documentaries to form the text-script pairs, but do not modify the scripts by ourselves (as inexperienced users). The details of forming the text-script pairs have been provided in Appendix C (**also see our first-round response to Q3**).

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a novel framework called RATV for automatically generating video montages from arbitrary text scripts. RATV retrieves and assembles video shots in a correct order using frozen visual and text CLIP encoders and a multimodal Transformer to learn the text-video joint representation in sequence-level. The Transformer termed sequence consistency Transformer is trained with two novel tasks, Cross-Modal Sequence Matching (CMSM) task and Chaotic Sequence Recovering (CSR) task for learning both the sequence coherence and sentence-shot alignment. Since there is no available benchmark for this task, the authors collect a new collection of diverse video-script pairs, Video-Script Pairs in Documentary (VSPD), and RATV outperforms baselines on this benchmark in terms of several retrieval metrics.

content.title: Response to Reviewer s74o
content.comment:
Thank you for the constructive comments and suggestions.

**Q1. [Table 2 does not provide results using Write-A-Video and Transcript-to-Video models finetuned on VSPD.]** \
**A1:** Sorry for the confusion. The results of Write-A-Video and Transcript-to-Video in Table 2 are indeed obtained by model finetuning on VSPD. The implemention details are given below:
* Due to the unavailable code and models, both Write-A-Video and Transcript-to-Video directly adopt the new state-of-the-art image-text model CLIP as the backbone for text-shot retrival, which is frozen during model training. That is, these two methods are initialized with CLIP just as our RATV for fair comparison. 
* With CLIP-based initialization (CLIP is frozen during training), the main difference between these two methods and our RATV lies in the strategy of arranging the retrieved shots. Concretely, Write-A-Video adopts pre-defined rules to arrange the retrieved shots. For better implemention, we carefully select the hyper-parameters (e.g., threshold and coeffcient) of the rules according to its validation performance on our VSPD dataset. Such hyper-parameter tuning can be considered as a kind of finetuning on VSPD. Moreover, Transcript-to-Video adopts beam-search based on a trained classifier to achieve the  goal of arranging the retrieved shots. We thus train the required classifier on VSPD for beam search. 

In conclusion, we have finetuned Write-A-Video and Transcript-to-Video on the VSPD dataset, and the results of these two methods shown in Table 2 have been obtained under fair comparison.

**Q2. [However, the code should be released for reproduction.]** \
**A2:** Thanks. We have released the code in the supplementary material.

content.title: General Response: Contributions and New Experiments
content.comment:
We sincerely appreciate all reviewers’ time and efforts in reviewing our paper. We are glad to find that reviewers generally recognized our contributions: 
* **Dataset.** Collecting and proposing **the first public** video montage generation benchmark [s74o, GsLm, 7B6W, kWC4], which will be very helpful to the community [s74o, GsLm].
* **Model.** Introducing a new way and cool idea to solve video montage generation task [7B6W, GsLm], and the proposed method makes sense [kWC4]. 
* **Experiment.** The experimental results and ablation study demonstarte the effectiveness of proposed method and support the paper’s motivation [s74o, 7B6W, kWC4].
* **Writing.** The paper is well-written and easy to read [s74o]; the paper is fairly clear to understand what is done [7B6W, kWC4].

And we also thank all reviewers for their insightful and constructive suggestions, which help a lot in further improving our paper. In addition to the pointwise responses below, we summarize supporting experiments added in the rebuttal according to reviewers’ suggestions.

**New Experiments** 
* The user study to show the impact of subjectivity [kWC4].
* Comparision among models trained with different length distributions of positive and negative samples [kWC4].

**Code/Dataset Availability**
* The code is provided in the supplementary material, and the dataset is avalibale at https://github.com/RATVDemo/RATV.

We hope that our pointwise responses below could clarify all reviewers’ confusion and alleviate all of their concerns. We'd like to thank all reviewers’ time again.
